extraction.name: ChartQA
extraction.description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering human-written and machine-generated questions on real-world charts.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four online sources, with chart images and associated metadata/data tables collected where available; human-authored QA pairs were collected via AMT, and additional QA pairs were generated from human-written chart summaries using T5 and filtered heuristically.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world charts from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD; for Pew only chart images were crawled, while for the other three sources underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions were extracted.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For machine-generated QA pairs, invalid questions were filtered out if the answer could not be found in the chart data table, and the machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected on Amazon Mechanical Turk by asking workers to write two questions per chart focused on compositional and visual reasoning, provide answers, and then have another annotator answer the same questions; disagreements were manually resolved. Additional QA pairs were generated from Statista summaries using fine-tuned T5 models for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Agreement between crowd workers was measured using exact match and additionally manually checked on 500 random samples to account for typos and lexical variations; machine-generated QA quality was manually analyzed on 1,250 QA pairs.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that the models could be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Topic distribution is uneven across sources, with politics especially common in the Pew subset.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark remains challenging due to human-written visual and logical reasoning questions; machine-generated questions can be invalid due to domain mismatch; performance drops when gold tables are unavailable because automatic data extraction from real-world charts is difficult.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating Chart Question Answering systems, including training, validation, and testing on human-written and machine-generated QA pairs.

name.evidence: In this work, we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries.

description.evidence: To address these limitations, we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9,608 human-written questions focusing on logical and visual reasoning questions.

url.evidence: Our code and dataset are publicly available athttps://github.com/vis-nlp/ChartQA

inLanguage.evidence: The goal of a Chart Question Answering (ChartQA) system is to help users by taking a chart and a natural language question as input and predicting the answer.

isLiveDataset.evidence: We randomly split both of the human-written (ChartQA-H) and machine generated (ChartQA-M) QA pairs into train, validation, and test sets as shown in Table 2.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: To ensure that our benchmark covers various topics and charts with a diverse range of styles, we crawled charts from four different sources: (i) Statista (statista.com) is an online platform that presents charts covering a variety of topics including economy, politics, and industry. (ii) The Pew research (pewresearch.org) publishes report about social and economic issues, demographic trends and public opinion with a wide variety of charts. (iii) Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org) is another platform that contains thousands of charts about different global issues such as economy, finance, and society. (iv) Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development or OECD (oecd.org) is a global organization which shares reports and data analysis for policymaking.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: To ensure that our benchmark covers various topics and charts with a diverse range of styles, we crawled charts from four different sources... We have two main annotations procedures: (i) collect human-authored QA pairs using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) and (ii) generate QA pairs from the Statista human-written summaries.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: For the Pew dataset, we only crawled chart images since the underlying data tables are not available. For the other three, we extracted the underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG file and associate text description.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To filter out such invalid questions, we developed a simple heuristic where we filter out the question if the answer cannot be found in the chart data table. ... Moreover, for the sake of fair evaluation, we manually cleaned the test set of the machine generated dataset by removing invalid questions.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: To create human-authored QA pairs, we designed an AMT task (see A.1 for details) in which we asked the crowdworkers to focus on two types of questions for each chart image: compositional and visual questions. ... For each chart, the workers provide two questions with the answers. The same questions are then answered by another annotator. If both workers’ answers exactly match, we consider the answer to be correct. Otherwise, we manually check the answers to select the final correct answer.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We have two main annotations procedures: (i) collect human-authored QA pairs using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) and (ii) generate QA pairs from the Statista human-written summaries.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Overall, the agreement between the crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. However, such exact match does not consider typos or lexical variations (e.g., 3$ vs. 3 dollars, 86.33 vs 86.3) that are common in human annotation. Hence, we have also manually checked the agreement on 500 random samples and found the agreement to be much higher (78.55%) when we consider typos and lexical variations.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: For each chart, the workers provide two questions with the answers. The same questions are then answered by another annotator.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: Specifically, we fine-tune a pre-trained T5 model on the SQuAD QA dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and apply to the human-written chart summaries that come with the charts from Statista to automatically generate questions that are human-like with sufficient lexical and syntactic variations.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Our models can be abused to mislead the public about the charts content and implications.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Politics is a common topic among all sources but particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4 %).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: However, the T5 question generation model may still generate invalid questions because of the mismatch in training and test domains. ... Finally, the performance of our models decreases when the gold data table was not given. This highlights the increasing challenge of automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diversity in styles.
